title: MITCHELL-RILEY SYNDROME
alt_titles: DIABETES, NEONATAL, WITH PANCREATIC HYPOPLASIA, INTESTINAL ATRESIA, AND GALLBLADDER APLASIA OR HYPOPLASIA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Mitchell-Riley syndrome (MTCHRS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RFX6 gene on chromosome 6q21-q22.

checks.claim: Mitchell-Riley syndrome (MTCHRS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RFX6 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Missense, splicing or frameshift mutations in RFX6 were found in five of the six available probands (Fig. 5e)
checks.explanation: Probands were homozygous, except proband 3, who was compound heterozygous. The authors named the condition Mitchell-Riley syndrome.

checks.claim: The RFX6 gene is located on chromosome 6q21-q22.
checks.evidence_quote: only RFX6, which falls in the largest segment at 6q21-22, had pancreas–enriched expression in the TiGER database
checks.explanation: The paper places RFX6 within the 6q21-22 segment.

paragraphs.text: Mitchell-Riley syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its main features are neonatal diabetes, a hypoplastic or annular pancreas, duodenal and/or jejunal atresia, and aplasia or hypoplasia of the gallbladder (Mitchell et al., 2004). Other features are intrahepatic cholestasis and intractable diarrhea that does not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement. Many affected infants have died in the first year of life (Smith et al., 2010; Sansbury et al., 2015). In some patients, diabetes does not appear until childhood (Sansbury et al., 2015).

checks.claim: Mitchell-Riley syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: In human infants with a similar autosomal recessive syndrome of neonatal diabetes, genetic mapping and subsequent sequencing identified mutations in the human RFX6 gene.
checks.explanation: The abstract calls the syndrome autosomal recessive.

checks.claim: The main features of Mitchell-Riley syndrome are neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, duodenal and/or jejunal atresia, and aplasia or hypoplasia of the gallbladder.
checks.evidence_quote: presented with neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal atresia, duodenal atresia and gall bladder aplasia or hypoaplasia.

checks.claim: Other features of Mitchell-Riley syndrome are intrahepatic cholestasis and intractable diarrhea that does not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement.
checks.evidence_quote: In addition, the syndrome involves hypoplastic gall bladder, and intractable diarrhea unresponsive to pancreatic enzyme replacement.
checks.explanation: The paper supports the intractable diarrhea, but it does not mention intrahepatic cholestasis.

checks.claim: Many infants affected with Mitchell-Riley syndrome have died in the first year of life.
checks.evidence_quote: Probands #1, 4 and 5 all died in the first few months of life
checks.explanation: Three of the five probands with mutations died in early infancy.

checks.claim: In some patients with Mitchell-Riley syndrome, diabetes does not appear until childhood.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we report the first cases of Mitchell–Riley syndrome in which the onset of diabetes occurred outside the neonatal period.
checks.explanation: Diabetes was diagnosed at 3 and 6 years.

paragraphs.text: Martínez-Frías et al. (1992) reported 2 sibs born to consanguineous parents. Both had low birth weight, tracheoesophageal fistula, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, a hypoplastic pancreas, and hypospadias. The authors suggested that this was a previously unreported autosomal recessive syndrome. Annerén et al. (1998) reported a lethal autosomal recessive syndrome with intrauterine growth retardation, intra- and extrahepatic biliary atresia, and esophageal and duodenal atresia. Gentile and Fiorente (1999) reported esophageal, duodenal, rectoanal, and biliary atresia, intestinal malrotation, a malformed or hypoplastic pancreas, and hypospadias. They considered this further evidence of a new, distinct syndrome. Galán-Gómez et al. (2007) described a female infant born to consanguineous parents. She had low birth weight, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, a hypoplastic pancreas, and intestinal malrotation, and she died 60 days after birth. Her karyotype was normal (46,XX).

paragraphs.text: Chappell et al. (2008) suggested that patients with neonatal diabetes, intestinal atresias, and gallbladder agenesis, and those with overlapping patterns such as the patients of Martínez-Frías et al. (1992), may have variations of the same syndrome. Martinovici et al. (2010) diagnosed Martínez-Frías syndrome in a newborn with intestinal atresia, gallbladder aplasia, and diabetes mellitus. Smith et al. (2010) disagreed. They noted that the original Martínez-Frías syndrome patients had esophageal atresia and hypospadias but no diabetes, and that no RFX6 mutation was found in the parents of 1 case of Martínez-Frías syndrome. On this basis they considered their patients with RFX6 mutations distinct from Martínez-Frías syndrome. They named the condition Mitchell-Riley syndrome after the 2 clinicians who first described it.

paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (2004) described 5 infants: 2 sib pairs from 2 families and 1 isolated case. One sib pair was born to consanguineous parents. The infants had neonatal diabetes, a hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal atresia, duodenal atresia, and aplasia or hypoplasia of the gallbladder. One patient had a milder form and survived without insulin. The other 4 children died in the first year of life despite aggressive medical management. Pancreatic tissue from 3 infants was studied by immunohistochemistry. It showed a few scattered chromogranin A-positive cell clusters but no insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin. Exocrine histology varied.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome whose diabetes was not diagnosed until the ages of 3 and 6 years. In both, a period of asymptomatic hyperglycemia of at least 1 year came before the diagnosis. The girl was born at 32 weeks' gestation with duodenal atresia, a jejunal web, and Meckel diverticulum. She was also found to have an absent gallbladder. She presented with diabetic ketoacidosis at age 3 years, with insulin below 2 microIU/ml and C-peptide of 0.023 ng/ml. The boy was born at 34 weeks' gestation with duodenal atresia and midgut malrotation. He presented with hyperglycemia (16.0 mmol/l) at age 6 years. Neither child had liver involvement, and islet autoantibodies were negative in both. Both were alive at age 9 years. The authors also reviewed 8 previously published patients with molecularly confirmed disease. All had duodenal atresia, 7 of 8 had gallbladder agenesis, and 7 of 8 had intrahepatic cholestasis. Five of the 8 had died, all within the first year of life.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) performed high-resolution homozygosity mapping in 2 probands, the offspring of first cousins and of second cousins. Only 3 homozygous-by-descent regions, totaling 24 Mb, were shared by both probands: on 2p15-p16, 6q21-q22, and 6q23. Of the 194 RefSeq genes in these regions, only RFX6, in the largest segment at 6q21-q22, showed pancreas-enriched expression in the TiGER database (Liu et al., 2008).

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) used deep sequencing to analyze the captured exons in the shared homozygous regions in proband 2. The only nonsynonymous variant found was a homozygous ser217-to-pro (S217P) mutation in RFX6. Direct sequencing of RFX6 found mutations in 5 of 6 probands, all inherited from carrier parents. Probands 1, 4, and 5 died in the first few months of life. Each was homozygous for a different mutation: a splice donor site mutation in intron 2 (IVS2+2T-C), an out-of-frame deletion in exon 7, or the missense mutation R181Q. Proband 3 was alive at age 9 years and intermittently off insulin. This patient was compound heterozygous for splice site mutations in intron 6 (IVS6+2T-G) and intron 1 (IVS1-12A-G). In autopsy pancreas from proband 1, the properly spliced transcript was not detected. In electrophoretic mobility shift assays, R181Q completely abolished DNA binding, whereas S217P only modestly reduced it. No RFX6 mutation was found in proband 6. DNA from this proband was not available, and the authors considered the case most likely a phenocopy.

Targeted next-generation sequencing, confirmed by Sanger sequencing, showed that both children were compound heterozygous for 2 nonsense mutations in RFX6: R726X in exon 17 and R866X in exon 18. The fathers were heterozygous for R726X, and the mothers were heterozygous for R866X. Both mutations had been inherited from the grandmothers.

It could therefore produce a partially truncated protein with a fully preserved DNA-binding domain. They suggested that this might explain the later onset of diabetes and the milder phenotype in their patients.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) generated Rfx6-null mice. The homozygous mice were born at the expected mendelian ratio but did not feed normally. They had gross bowel distension from small bowel obstruction and died within 2 days of birth. Some had a smaller pancreas. The mutant pancreas still contained many endocrine cells, but none expressed insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, or ghrelin, and pancreatic polypeptide-expressing cells were increased. Neurogenin-3 expression was not affected, whereas Arx, Irx2, Pax6, Mafa, Neurod1, and Pdx1 expression was reduced. Rfx6 formed a heterodimeric DNA-binding complex with Rfx3.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) studied 2 Turkish double first cousins with MTCHRS whose diabetes began at ages 3 and 6 years. Targeted next-generation sequencing, confirmed by Sanger sequencing, showed that both were compound heterozygous for 2 nonsense mutations in RFX6. One was a c.2176C-T transition in exon 17, resulting in an arg726-to-ter (R726X) substitution. The other was a c.2596C-T transition in exon 18, resulting in an arg866-to-ter (R866X) substitution. The fathers carried R726X, the mothers carried R866X, and both mutations had been inherited from the grandmothers. R726X is predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay. R866X lies within 50 nucleotides of the last exon-exon boundary and is predicted to escape it.
